Boogie-Woogie

A left hand that walks: eight to the bar on the blues

Open the Boogie-woogie style in the Backing Track

What it is

Blues piano with a left hand that never stops: eight notes to the bar, swung, repeating one figure up and down the chord while the right hand plays riffs, tremolos and blue notes against it. It is almost always a 12-bar blues.

Boogie-woogie and stride are close relations: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a band into the left hand, and the same pianists often played both. Stride’s left hand leaps between bass and chord on the beats; boogie-woogie’s walks along the bass in eighth notes. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

A little history

The style began in the lumber, turpentine and railroad camps of Texas and Louisiana in the first years of the 1900s, played on “barrelhouse” pianos in the camps’ bars, and travelled north with the migration. In Chicago in the 1920s it was the music of rent parties, as stride was in Harlem. Pinetop Smith’s Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie (1928) gave the style its name; Jimmy Yancey, Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons played it in Chicago.

In December 1938 the producer John Hammond put Ammons, Lewis and Pete Johnson on stage at Carnegie Hall in the From Spirituals to Swing concert, and boogie-woogie became a national craze. Big bands arranged it (Count Basie’s Boogie Woogie, Tommy Dorsey’s version of Pinetop’s piece), and the Andrews Sisters sang it. Its eight-to-the-bar bass went into jump blues, rhythm and blues and early rock and roll: Chuck Berry’s guitar plays a boogie left hand.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths walking up the chord and back down, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd, every bar. The pianist’s left hand, on the bass.
  • Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords against the bass.
  • Drums: Blues shuffle: swung eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
  • Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Boogie-woogie pianists have dozens of left-hand patterns (rolling octaves, the Yancey bass, broken sixths) and their right hands play the lead. The band’s bassist has one pattern and its pianist one riff, so a melody or a solo on top is your part.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Meade Lux Lewis, Honky Tonk Train Blues 1927 A train in the left hand, cross-rhythms in the right.
Pinetop Smith, Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie 1928 The record that named the style; Smith calls out to the dancers.
Albert Ammons, Boogie Woogie Stomp 1936 The walking left hand at full power.
Count Basie, Boogie Woogie (with Jimmy Rushing) 1936 Boogie-woogie from a small swing band.
Big Joe Turner and Pete Johnson, Roll ’Em Pete 1938 Boogie-woogie under a blues shouter: a short step to rock and roll.
Jimmy Yancey, Yancey Stomp 1939 A lighter, older Chicago style.

More recent

Recording Year Listen for
Jerry Lee Lewis, Whole Lotta Shakin’ Goin’ On 1957 The boogie left hand in rock and roll.

Sources

  • Peter J. Silvester, A Left Hand Like God: A History of Boogie-Woogie Piano (Quartet, 1988).
  • Ted Gioia, The History of Jazz (Oxford, 1997), on Chicago and the 1938 Carnegie Hall concert.
  • Riccardo Scivales, Jazz Piano: The Left Hand (Ekay, 1990), on stride and boogie-woogie left hands.
